Deadly Waters (Shark Nets)

By: Beth Neale | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
An investigation into KwaZulu-Natal’s shark nets reveals a publicly funded culling system still killing thousands of marine animals — but now, the public is fighting back.

Unique Selling Point:
What sets Deadly Waters apart is its timing and urgency: this year marked the first fatal shark incident on the KwaZulu-Natal coast in over 30 years, reigniting public fear — and the justification for keeping lethal shark nets and drum lines in place. But the real twist is that this system, publicly funded and decades old, isn’t just ineffective — it’s being actively challenged by the public. The Marine Liberation Society, an anonymous activist group, went so far as to impersonate the Sharks Board to expose the truth and stir national debate. Their bold campaign reflects a tipping point: ordinary citizens, scientists, and survivors are uniting to dismantle a dangerous myth. This insert doesn’t just reveal the ecological cost of outdated policy — it captures a groundswell of resistance, giving voice to those demanding real change.

Summary:
Sharks have long inspired fear, especially along South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal coast. In the wake of a rare fatal shark incident during this year’s sardine run — the first in over 30 years — Carte Blanche investigates a system designed to protect beachgoers: the shark nets and drum lines maintained by the KwaZulu-Natal Sharks Board. But what begins as a safety measure unravels into a story of outdated policy, ecological devastation, and public deception. We join scientists, conservationists, and even a shark attack survivor as they guide us through the reality of these culling devices — responsible for the deaths of more than 33,000 sharks, including threatened and protected species. But the toll doesn’t end there: more than 2,000 dolphins, 2,000 turtles, 8,000 rays, and even migrating whales have been caught as bycatch. The insert follows a journey of rethinking sharks — exposing the myth of the "man-eater," and showcasing how individuals and groups, like the Marine Liberation Society, are going to extraordinary lengths to challenge the current system. As pressure mounts, the question becomes unavoidable: if there are better solutions, why are we still killing sharks in the name of safety — even inside Marine Protected Areas?

Press Release:


Deadly Waters

Sharks: they’re often reviled and feared as cold-blooded predators. But in this story, they are the victims… of a decades-old, publicly
funded system
that critics say is as environmentally disastrous as it is outdated. Shark nets and drum lines stretch for kilometres
along the KwaZulu-Natal coastline and into Marine Protected Areas, lethal not only to sharks, but dolphins, turtles, and rays. And now, the nets and hooks are coming under public attack. As pressure mounts, supporters double down, while activists turn to increasingly
controversial methods. Is it time to rethink our relationship with sharks?

Producer: Beth Neale | Presenter: Lourensa Eckard

Script:


(Craig Lambinon, NSRI) “... search and rescue and water police diving services, located and recovered the body of a man… in an apparent shark incident. The body recovered by police divers, appears to show signs of obvious shark wounds that are being investigated…”
(Lourensa) And now I have to get in there?
(Lourensa) Sharks.
(Lourensa) I’m shaking now.
(Lourensa) A fear so great, it became government policy. Lethal fishing gear, deployed for kilometres along the coast.
(Geremy Cliff) Shark nets are effective because they reduce the number of sharks.
(Lourensa) But, as shark numbers dwindle, the debate around a deadly deterrent is intensifying.
(Lourensa) How far are you willing to go to protect these marine animals?
(Lourensa) And obscure activist groups are using increasingly controversial methods to sway public opinion.
(Marine Liberation Society) Anybody that joins us has to be willing to be arrested.
(Lourensa) In May this year, a tagged juvenile great white was found dead on a baited hook, known as a drumline, in KwaZulu Natal.
(Lourensa) It sparked intense criticism.
(Lourensa) In 1991, we became the first country in the world to protect great whites.
(Lourensa) But KZN’s state-run Sharks Board is legally allowed to deploy nets and drumlines to catch them.
(Lourensa) It’s their job, they say, to manage bather safety.
(Lourensa) They target three potentially dangerous species — tiger, bull and great white sharks.
(Lourensa) But, for every one target shark, about five non-target animals are also caught; most don’t survive.
(Lourensa) It’s a statistic that’s concerned conservationists for years.
(Lourensa) But so outraged has one, relatively unknown activist group become, that it’s turned to unconventional methods to highlight the issue.
(Lourensa) When a newspaper article claimed that the shark nets in KwaZulu-Natal were finally being replaced by a non-lethal alternative, it sparked a celebration… until people realised it was a hoax.
(Lourensa) It turns out, the article – which claimed the current methods would be replaced by non-lethal alternatives - was planted by a secretive organisation calling itself “The Marine Liberation Society”. It was labelled highly unethical, but the MLS is unrepentant.
(MLS) We created a fabricated story in which the KwaZulu-Natal sharks board took credit for the fact that their outdated culling system, which originated in the 1950s, was in fact responsible for a great loss in terms of marine life.
(Lourensa) So you essentially faked a government press release?
(MLS) That is correct.
(Lourensa) Curious about their motives, size, and influence, we tracked them down and asked for an interview.
(Lourensa) After a seemingly endless back-and-and-forth trying to prove we were who we said we were, we were told to speak to this man. He asked us to keep his identity and voice hidden.
(Lourensa) Some people would say that you knowingly deceived the public.
(MLS) Compared to the suffering that the animals go through, I couldn't be bothered.
Ultimately our job is to shine light wherever it needs to go in order for this injustice to stop.
(Lourensa) The MLS is a volunteer direct-action group. We’ve been unable to verify how big their membership is or how influential they are, but they say the fake article is just the beginning.
(MLS) People have had enough. And it's not one or just two emotional animal activists. It's communities that have built their lives, their livelihoods around these animals.
(Lourensa) The MLS claims research values a live great white at around R10 million.
(MLS) So every time you take a shark out of circulation, you're actually costing our economy a lot of money. It's time to start trialling new systems. It's time to start implementing new systems.
(Lourensa) Our conversation with the MLS came just months after a rare fatal shark attack. In July, a fisherman was killed at an unprotected South Coast beach. The debate around nets and drumlines was re-ignited.
(Lourensa) Geremy Cliff, now a conservation consultant, worked at the Sharks Board for 36 years.
(GEREMY) There hasn't been a fatal shark attack along the Durban beachfront for the last 73 years. So I think that gives you a pretty good indication that the shark nets have certainly been incredibly effective.
(Lourensa) Is the intention then to actually catch the shark. It's not to be a barrier for the shark to somehow see and stay away from?
(Lourensa) It was never designed to be a physical barrier at all. Sharks will swim either over the top, underneath, or round the sides.
(Lourensa) So is it effective because it lowers the number of sharks?
(GEREMY) Yes.
(Lourensa) By killing them?
(GEREMY) By killing them.
(Lourensa) Up to 40% of sharks are caught on the beach side of the nets — on their way out, not in. Drumlines, large baited hooks, are more selective in targeting only sharks.
(Lourensa) So is the trade-off then, to keep people safe, sharks unfortunately need to die?
(Geremy) Unfortunately. It's very difficult. The. The sea belongs to sharks. And it's just unfortunate that we only have lethal means at our disposal at this stage.
(Joshua Pons) So we’re here at Zinkwazi Beach…
(Lourensa) Last year, a dead great white shark was filmed on the KZN North Coast. It was killed by a drumline inside what’s known as a Marine Protected Area.
(Joshua Pons) This is a Marine Protected Area, so there’s a whole lot of rules that you have to follow.
(Lourensa) A Marine Protected Area, or MPA, is designated for the conservation of sea life.
(Lourensa) There are five along the KZN coast, but the Sharks Board has nets and drum lines installed in three of them.
(Joshua Pons) This is an offence comparable to rhino poaching.
(Lourensa) Is marine life really protected, if you have drum lines and shark nets?
(GEREMY) It is a huge issue. Those areas were only relatively recently declared Marine Protected Areas. The Sharks Board would never have deliberately installed gear in an existing MPA.
(Lourensa) Was it difficult for you during your time with the sharks board to reconcile with the ecological damage done by these, these practices?
(Geremy) It is. It's very difficult to experiment because you're dealing with human life. But I believe the Sharks Board has done a huge amount to reduce catches. And obviously then reduce environmental impact.
(Lourensa) Under Geremy, 45 kilometres of nets were reduced to 21 kilometres, with drumlines taking their place — and annual catches more than halved.
(Lourensa) It seems pressure to continue bringing down those numbers is growing. I asked Geremy if he thought that was why the Shark’s Board was reluctant to meet us.
(Geremy) Look, it's not a new pressure. But the fact remains is that there has been a growing number of people who are against killing sharks to protect people. I can't speak for them.
(Lourensa) This is the KwaZulu-Natal Sharks Board. They've declined our request for an on-camera interview. And when we asked to film inside, they sent us this statement, “Unfortunately, filming will not be permitted at our premises at this point in time, as this matter still needs to be given due consideration, as your intention to film would by implication result in the publication of such content." I'm not exactly sure what this means.
(Lourensa) The Sharks Board answers to Provincial MEC, Musa Zondi. He also declined our request for an interview after seeing our questions.
(MLS) Our job as the MLS is, is to shine a light on the Sharks Board And, we want to make it really uncomfortable for them.
(Lourensa) Ultimately, a decision on the continued use of nets and drum lines will fall to the Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment - currently Dion George.
(Lourensa) In a statement, he says there are no proven non-lethal methods to replace them, adding that the aim is to gradually introduce proven new technologies.
(Lourensa) Say, for example, we did away with these nets and drumlines and there was a fatal shark attack. You know, people would point fingers towards that, that that minister and politician immediately.
(MLS) One shark attack? And this is the problem with sharks. It our perception. Sharks present a negligible risk to humans.
(Lourensa) Worldwide, sharks kill about six people a year on average. Last year, there were four fatalities.
(Lourensa) Do you think there's an attempt at indoctrination by the sharks board in terms of also instilling a sense of fear?
(MLS) Absolutely. If the public no longer believes that sharks are these scary monsters, their funding will dry up.
(Lourensa) Last year the Sharks Board’s revenue was approximately R116-million, the majority of that is from public funding.
(Lourensa) The Sharks Board responded in writing, rejecting claims of fear mongering, saying its focus is on protecting beachgoers and supporting the coastal economy.
(Lourena) The Sharks Board facility is open to the public.
(Lourensa) So, I first visited the Sharks Board as a child. This was many years ago, and I remember feeling absolutely terrified after that visit. Now I've just been inside and nothing much has changed. I'm still very much afraid of sharks. And there's no mention of the amount of sharks and other marine animals that die as a result of these shark nets and drumlines.
(Lourensa) It’s said, we should face our fears, so I decided to do just that.
(Lourensa) Walter Bernardis is a pioneer of shark diving in these parts.
(Walter) It’s unacceptable to have, what's little left of our resources, being destroyed by those curtains of death and the drumlines.
It’s time for them to come up with a more eco-friendly system.
(Lourensa) Oh no! Sjoe!
(Lourensa) We’ve seen the first shark, we’re going to get in shortly.
(Lourensa) That seems a bit big, Walter!
(Lourensa) Do I have anything to fear when I get into the water just now?
(Walter) Look, you are getting in the water with the apex predators. So, if you just observe the two basic rules: number one, don’t look like food; and number two, don’t act like food.
(Lourensa) I’m going in with my producer who has spent years swimming with sharks.
(Producer Beth Neale) This is where you’ve really got to trust your producer.
(Lourensa) With my life.
(Lourensa) Here goes nothing…
(Lourensa) That is amazing!
(Lourensa) It’s just the most amazing thing. They felt so calm. I didn’t feel afraid for one minute. And to just see them up close, they are the most majestic animals I think I’ve ever seen.
(MLS) I know change will come. The question is just when it will come. A world without sharks is much worse than a world with sharks.

Unique Selling Point: What sets Deadly Waters apart is its timing and urgency: this year marked the first fatal shark incident on the KwaZulu-Natal coast in over 30 years, reigniting public fear — and the justification for keeping lethal shark nets and drum lines in place. But the real twist is that this system, publicly funded and decades old, isn’t just ineffective — it’s being actively challenged by the public. The Marine Liberation Society, an anonymous activist group, went so far as to impersonate the Sharks Board to expose the truth and stir national debate. Summary: Sharks have long inspired fear, especially along South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal coast. In the wake of a rare fatal shark incident during this year’s sardine run — the first in over 30 years — Carte Blanche investigates a system designed to protect beachgoers: the shark nets and drum lines maintained by the KwaZulu-Natal Sharks Board. But what begins as a safety measure unravels into a story of outdated policy, ecological devastation, and public deception. We join scientists, conservationists, and even a shark attack survivor as they guide us through the reality of these culling devices — responsible for the deaths of more than 33,000 sharks, including threatened and protected species. But the toll doesn’t end there: more than 2,000 dolphins, 2,000 turtles, 8,000 rays, and even migrating whales have been caught as bycatch. The insert follows a journey of rethinking sharks — exposing the myth of the "man-eater," and showcasing how individuals and groups, like the Marine Liberation Society, are going to extraordinary lengths to challenge the current system. As pressure mounts, the question becomes unavoidable: if there are better solutions, why are we still killing sharks in the name of safety — even inside Marine Protected Areas? references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 07 September 2025 - Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 08 September 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: Deadly Waters Sharks: they’re often reviled and feared as cold-blooded predators. But in this story, they are the victims… of a decades-old, publicly funded system that critics say is as environmentally disastrous as it is outdated. Shark nets and drum lines stretch for kilometres along the KwaZulu-Natal coastline and into Marine Protected Areas, lethal not only to sharks, but dolphins, turtles, and rays. And now, the nets and hooks are coming under public attack. As pressure mounts, supporters double down, while activists turn to increasingly controversial methods. Is it time to rethink our relationship with sharks? Producer: Beth Neale | Presenter: Lourensa Eckard Script: (Craig Lambinon, NSRI) “... search and rescue and water police diving services, located and recovered the body of a man… in an apparent shark incident. The body recovered by police divers, appears to show signs of obvious shark wounds that are being investigated…” (Lourensa) And now I have to get in there? (Lourensa) Sharks. (Lourensa) I’m shaking now. (Lourensa) A fear so great, it became government policy. Lethal fishing gear, deployed for kilometres along the coast. (Geremy Cliff) Shark nets are effective because they reduce the number of sharks. (Lourensa) But, as shark numbers dwindle, the debate around a deadly deterrent is intensifying. (Lourensa) How far are you willing to go to protect these marine animals? (Lourensa) And obscure activist groups are using increasingly controversial methods to sway public opinion. (Marine Liberation Society) Anybody that joins us has to be willing to be arrested. (Lourensa) In May this year, a tagged juvenile great white was found dead on a baited hook, known as a drumline, in KwaZulu Natal. (Lourensa) It sparked intense criticism. (Lourensa) In 1991, we became the first country in the world to protect great whites. (Lourensa) But KZN’s state-run Sharks Board is legally allowed to deploy nets and drumlines to catch them. (Lourensa) It’s their job, they say, to manage bather safety. (Lourensa) They target three potentially dangerous species — tiger, bull and great white sharks. (Lourensa) But, for every one target shark, about five non-target animals are also caught; most don’t survive. (Lourensa) It’s a statistic that’s concerned conservationists for years. (Lourensa) But so outraged has one, relatively unknown activist group become, that it’s turned to unconventional methods to highlight the issue. (Lourensa) When a newspaper article claimed that the shark nets in KwaZulu-Natal were finally being replaced by a non-lethal alternative, it sparked a celebration… until people realised it was a hoax. (Lourensa) It turns out, the article – which claimed the current methods would be replaced by non-lethal alternatives - was planted by a secretive organisation calling itself “The Marine Liberation Society”. It was labelled highly unethical, but the MLS is unrepentant. (MLS) We created a fabricated story in which the KwaZulu-Natal sharks board took credit for the fact that their outdated culling system, which originated in the 1950s, was in fact responsible for a great loss in terms of marine life. (Lourensa) So you essentially faked a government press release? (MLS) That is correct. (Lourensa) Curious about their motives, size, and influence, we tracked them down and asked for an interview. (Lourensa) After a seemingly endless back-and-and-forth trying to prove we were who we said we were, we were told to speak to this man. He asked us to keep his identity and voice hidden. (Lourensa) Some people would say that you knowingly deceived the public. (MLS) Compared to the suffering that the animals go through, I couldn't be bothered. Ultimately our job is to shine light wherever it needs to go in order for this injustice to stop. (Lourensa) The MLS is a volunteer direct-action group. We’ve been unable to verify how big their membership is or how influential they are, but they say the fake article is just the beginning. (MLS) People have had enough. And it's not one or just two emotional animal activists. It's communities that have built their lives, their livelihoods around these animals. (Lourensa) The MLS claims research values a live great white at around R10 million. (MLS) So every time you take a shark out of circulation, you're actually costing our economy a lot of money. It's time to start trialling new systems. It's time to start implementing new systems. (Lourensa) Our conversation with the MLS came just months after a rare fatal shark attack. In July, a fisherman was killed at an unprotected South Coast beach. The debate around nets and drumlines was re-ignited. (Lourensa) Geremy Cliff, now a conservation consultant, worked at the Sharks Board for 36 years. (GEREMY) There hasn't been a fatal shark attack along the Durban beachfront for the last 73 years. So I think that gives you a pretty good indication that the shark nets have certainly been incredibly effective. (Lourensa) Is the intention then to actually catch the shark. It's not to be a barrier for the shark to somehow see and stay away from? (Lourensa) It was never designed to be a physical barrier at all. Sharks will swim either over the top, underneath, or round the sides. (Lourensa) So is it effective because it lowers the number of sharks? (GEREMY) Yes. (Lourensa) By killing them? (GEREMY) By killing them. (Lourensa) Up to 40% of sharks are caught on the beach side of the nets — on their way out, not in. Drumlines, large baited hooks, are more selective in targeting only sharks. (Lourensa) So is the trade-off then, to keep people safe, sharks unfortunately need to die? (Geremy) Unfortunately. It's very difficult. The. The sea belongs to sharks. And it's just unfortunate that we only have lethal means at our disposal at this stage. (Joshua Pons) So we’re here at Zinkwazi Beach… (Lourensa) Last year, a dead great white shark was filmed on the KZN North Coast. It was killed by a drumline inside what’s known as a Marine Protected Area. (Joshua Pons) This is a Marine Protected Area, so there’s a whole lot of rules that you have to follow. (Lourensa) A Marine Protected Area, or MPA, is designated for the conservation of sea life. (Lourensa) There are five along the KZN coast, but the Sharks Board has nets and drum lines installed in three of them. (Joshua Pons) This is an offence comparable to rhino poaching. (Lourensa) Is marine life really protected, if you have drum lines and shark nets? (GEREMY) It is a huge issue. Those areas were only relatively recently declared Marine Protected Areas. The Sharks Board would never have deliberately installed gear in an existing MPA. (Lourensa) Was it difficult for you during your time with the sharks board to reconcile with the ecological damage done by these, these practices? (Geremy) It is. It's very difficult to experiment because you're dealing with human life. But I believe the Sharks Board has done a huge amount to reduce catches. And obviously then reduce environmental impact. (Lourensa) Under Geremy, 45 kilometres of nets were reduced to 21 kilometres, with drumlines taking their place — and annual catches more than halved. (Lourensa) It seems pressure to continue bringing down those numbers is growing. I asked Geremy if he thought that was why the Shark’s Board was reluctant to meet us. (Geremy) Look, it's not a new pressure. But the fact remains is that there has been a growing number of people who are against killing sharks to protect people. I can't speak for them. (Lourensa) This is the KwaZulu-Natal Sharks Board. They've declined our request for an on-camera interview. And when we asked to film inside, they sent us this statement, “Unfortunately, filming will not be permitted at our premises at this point in time, as this matter still needs to be given due consideration, as your intention to film would by implication result in the publication of such content." I'm not exactly sure what this means. (Lourensa) The Sharks Board answers to Provincial MEC, Musa Zondi. He also declined our request for an interview after seeing our questions. (MLS) Our job as the MLS is, is to shine a light on the Sharks Board And, we want to make it really uncomfortable for them. (Lourensa) Ultimately, a decision on the continued use of nets and drum lines will fall to the Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment - currently Dion George. (Lourensa) In a statement, he says there are no proven non-lethal methods to replace them, adding that the aim is to gradually introduce proven new technologies. (Lourensa) Say, for example, we did away with these nets and drumlines and there was a fatal shark attack. You know, people would point fingers towards that, that that minister and politician immediately. (MLS) One shark attack? And this is the problem with sharks. It our perception. Sharks present a negligible risk to humans. (Lourensa) Worldwide, sharks kill about six people a year on average. Last year, there were four fatalities. (Lourensa) Do you think there's an attempt at indoctrination by the sharks board in terms of also instilling a sense of fear? (MLS) Absolutely. If the public no longer believes that sharks are these scary monsters, their funding will dry up. (Lourensa) Last year the Sharks Board’s revenue was approximately R116-million, the majority of that is from public funding. (Lourensa) The Sharks Board responded in writing, rejecting claims of fear mongering, saying its focus is on protecting beachgoers and supporting the coastal economy. (Lourena) The Sharks Board facility is open to the public. (Lourensa) So, I first visited the Sharks Board as a child. This was many years ago, and I remember feeling absolutely terrified after that visit. Now I've just been inside and nothing much has changed. I'm still very much afraid of sharks. And there's no mention of the amount of sharks and other marine animals that die as a result of these shark nets and drumlines. (Lourensa) It’s said, we should face our fears, so I decided to do just that. (Lourensa) Walter Bernardis is a pioneer of shark diving in these parts. (Walter) It’s unacceptable to have, what's little left of our resources, being destroyed by those curtains of death and the drumlines. It’s time for them to come up with a more eco-friendly system. (Lourensa) Oh no! Sjoe! (Lourensa) We’ve seen the first shark, we’re going to get in shortly. (Lourensa) That seems a bit big, Walter! (Lourensa) Do I have anything to fear when I get into the water just now? (Walter) Look, you are getting in the water with the apex predators. So, if you just observe the two basic rules: number one, don’t look like food; and number two, don’t act like food. (Lourensa) I’m going in with my producer who has spent years swimming with sharks. (Producer Beth Neale) This is where you’ve really got to trust your producer. (Lourensa) With my life. (Lourensa) Here goes nothing… (Lourensa) That is amazing! (Lourensa) It’s just the most amazing thing. They felt so calm. I didn’t feel afraid for one minute. And to just see them up close, they are the most majestic animals I think I’ve ever seen. (MLS) I know change will come. The question is just when it will come. A world without sharks is much worse than a world with sharks.

In the wake of a rare fatal shark incident during this year’s sardine run — the first in over 30 years — Carte Blanche investigates a system designed to protect beachgoers: the shark nets and drum lines maintained by the KwaZulu-Natal Sharks Board. But what begins as a safety measure unravels into a story of outdated policy, ecological devastation, and public deception. We join scientists, conservationists, and even a shark attack survivor as they guide us through the reality of these culling devices — responsible for the deaths of more than 33,000 sharks, including threatened and protected species. But the toll doesn’t end there: more than 2,000 dolphins, 2,000 turtles, 8,000 rays, and even migrating whales have been caught as bycatch. The insert follows a journey of rethinking sharks — exposing the myth of the "man-eater," and showcasing how individuals and groups, like the Marine Liberation Society, are going to extraordinary lengths to challenge the current system. As pressure mounts, the question becomes unavoidable: if there are better solutions, why are we still killing sharks in the name of safety — even inside Marine Protected Areas?
